alt: A tree diagram. The nervous system divides into the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) and the peripheral nervous system (all other nerves). The peripheral system divides into the somatic system (senses and voluntary movement) and the autonomic system (involuntary functions), which has sympathetic (fight or flight) and parasympathetic (rest and digest) branches.
caption: CNS decides; PNS carries messages. The autonomic branch runs involuntary functions.

alt: Three linked steps: a threat is perceived, the sympathetic branch is activated and the adrenal glands release adrenaline. The body changes: heart rate and breathing rise, pupils dilate, blood goes to the muscles and digestion slows. When the threat passes, the parasympathetic branch returns the body to rest.
caption: Sympathetic activation and adrenaline prepare the body; the parasympathetic branch calms it.

alt: Two rows of three steps. Common sense: see a bear, feel afraid, then the heart races. James-Lange: see a bear, the body reacts, then we interpret that change as fear. Evaluation cards: panic after a near miss supports the theory; similar bodily changes across emotions and emotions reported after spinal cord injury challenge it.
caption: James-Lange reverses common sense: the body reacts first and the emotion is our interpretation.

alt: A presynaptic axon terminal with an electrical impulse and vesicles of neurotransmitter faces a postsynaptic neuron across a synapse. Neurotransmitter crosses the gap and binds to receptors. Four steps: impulse to the terminal, release from vesicles, binding to receptors, and excitation or inhibition of the next neuron.
caption: The impulse is electrical along the neuron; a chemical neurotransmitter crosses the gap.

alt: Two pairs of neurons. Rarely active together, they share a thin, weak connection; after repeated activity together, a thick, stronger connection. Cards explain cell assemblies, that learning physically changes the brain, and that frequently used pathways become more efficient.
caption: Repeated activity strengthens connections: learning physically changes the brain.

after: ## Brain structure and localisation of function
alt: A schematic side view of the brain with the frontal, parietal, occipital and temporal lobes and the cerebellum. Labels mark the motor area at the back of the frontal lobe, the somatosensory area at the front of the parietal lobe, the visual area in the occipital lobe, the auditory area and Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe, and Broca's area in the frontal lobe.
caption: Particular areas carry out particular jobs; each side of the brain serves the opposite side of the body.

alt: A table compares scans: CT combines X-rays to show structure; PET uses an injected radioactive tracer and fMRI detects blood oxygen changes to show activity. A brain schematic for Tulving's gold study shows episodic memories linked to the frontal cortex and semantic memories to the back of the cortex.
caption: CT shows structure; PET and fMRI show activity. Tulving linked memory types to different areas.
